extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, legal and moral theory, and Hobbes' Leviathan
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Hobbes' normative criteria about law, crime, excuses, degrees of guilt, and punishment from Chapters XXVII–XXVIII of Leviathan. Focused on Hobbes' definitions and conditional rules for when actions are crimes, what excuses/attenuations apply, and what constitutes punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Law and Charter
rubrics_metrics.description: Charters are Donations of the Soveraign; and not Lawes, but exemptions from Law. The phrase of a Law is Jubeo, Injungo, I Command; the phrase of a Charter is Dedi, Concessi, I Have Given, I Have Granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is given or granted is not forced on the recipient by a law; a Law may bind all subjects of a commonwealth, whereas a Liberty or Charter is only to one man or some part of the people. Saying all people have liberty in any case is to say no law was made or it is abrogated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Sinne
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sinne, is not onely a Transgression of a Law, but also any Contempt of the Legislator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sin may consist in commission of a forbidden fact, speaking forbidden words, omission of commanded acts, or even in the intention or purpose to transgress. Mere imagination or delight in a fiction (e.g., imagining another's goods) is not a sin unless resolved into intent to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Crime
rubrics_metrics.description: A Crime, is a sinne, consisting in the Committing (by Deed, or Word) of that which the Law forbiddeth, or the Omission of what it hath commanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every Crime is a sin, but not every sin a crime. Intentions alone (that never appear outwardly) are sins but provide no ground for humane accusation. Crime requires an outward act or word making the intention perceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where no civil law exists, there is no crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Law ceaseth, Sinne ceaseth; the Civill Law ceasing, Crimes cease, since there is no place for Accusation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only natural law remains, violations may be sins but not crimes punishable by civil authority; each man becomes his own judge, accused only by conscience. This applies also when sovereign power ceaseth (no protection from law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the Law of Nature excuseth no man
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the Law of Nature Excuseth No Man; every man that hath attained the use of Reason is supposed to know it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wherever a man goes, acting contrary to natural law is a crime. Example: introducing doctrines that tend to disobedience of local laws is punishable even if the teacher believes them true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the Civil Law sometimes excuseth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the Civill Law shall excuse a man in a strange country, till it be declared to him; because, till then no Civill Law is binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the civil law of one's own country is not sufficiently declared such that a person could know it by reasonable effort, ignorance may be a valid excuse; mere negligence to inquire is not an excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the Sovereign excuseth not
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the Soveraign Power, in the place of a man's ordinary residence, Excuseth him not; because he ought to take notice of the Power by which he hath been protected there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects must recognize the sovereign authority under which they live; claiming ignorance of that sovereignty is not a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of the penalty excuseth not
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of the Penalty, where the Law is declared, Excuseth no man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment is a known consequence of law violation; voluntarily acting entails accepting known consequences. If the penalty is not yet determined, the offender is subject to arbitrary punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishments declared before the fact excuse from greater punishments after it
rubrics_metrics.description: But when a penalty is either annexed to the Crime in the Law itself, or hath been usually inflicted in like cases; there the Delinquent is Excused from a greater penalty afterwards inflicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a punishment was known and insufficient to deter, adding a greater punishment after the fact is unjust because the law tempted or deceived. Known lesser punishment reduces culpability for later excessive punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ex post facto law can make a past fact a crime
rubrics_metrics.description: No Law, made after a Fact done, can make it a Crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A positive law cannot obligate retroactively. However, if a law forbidding a fact existed before the fact, the actor is liable to the penalty ordained at the time (or arbitrary punishment if none specified).

rubrics_metrics.name: False principles of right and wrong cause crime
rubrics_metrics.description: From defect in Reasoning (Errour), men violate the laws by presumption of false principles (e.g., 'Justice is but a vain word', or that successful wrongdoing makes it lawful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If people take patterns of history or the success of wrongdoers as justification, they treat justice as contingent on fortune, thereby enabling crimes that destabilize commonwealth peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: False teachers mis-interpreting the law of nature cause crime
rubrics_metrics.description: False Teachers that either mis-interpret the Law of Nature, making it repugnant to the Civil Law, or teach doctrines inconsistent with duty, are causes of crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority of teachers can propagate error; teachings that conflict with civil duty encourage disobedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous inferences from true principles cause crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Erroneous Inferences from True Principles happen with hasty men who overvalue their understanding and precipitate judgment, leading to criminal actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those in positions of private or public administration who act from such error cannot rely on it as excuse—public duties require study and care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vain-glory and presumption of superiority cause crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Vain-glory or foolish over-rating of one's worth leads people to presume punishments shouldn't apply to them and thus commit crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption produces contempt of law and susceptibility to anger and other passions that create crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of riches as cause of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who value themselves by wealth adventure on Crimes hoping to escape punishment by corrupting justice or buying pardon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wealth-based presumption of impunity aggravates culpability and contributes to public corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption due to friends or popular support causes crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Many potent kindred or popular reputation lead men to violate laws from hope of resisting enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social power and networks that promise protective influence increase likelihood and gravity of crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: False wisdom (overconfidence in craft) causes crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with a false opinion of their wisdom take upon them to question governors and deceive neighbors; this presumption leads to craft and fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such people often provoke civil disorder and are mistaken about long-term benefits of their schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatred, lust, ambition, covetousness are causes of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions like Hate, Lust, Ambition, and Covetousnesse are obvious sources of crime; their effects cannot be hindered without extraordinary reason or strict punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These passions are natural and frequent; their prevention relies on continual use of reason or severity in punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear can sometimes cause crime; only present bodily fear justifies
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear sometimes causes crimes, but only the fear of corporeal hurt (present and unavoidable) can justify acts like killing in immediate self-defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear of non-corporeal or future harm (reputation, imagined threats, dreams, or superstitions) does not excuse breaking law; killing because of inferred future threat when protection is available is a crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes vary in degree; excuse and extenuation possible
rubrics_metrics.description: All Crimes are not of the same alloy; there is room for total excuse (removing nature of crime) and for extenuation (making a great crime less).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoic claim that all crimes equally unjust is rejected; differences in motive, circumstance, and effect matter to culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total excuses: lack of means to know the law; children and madmen
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of means to know the Law totally Excuseth; only Children and Madmen are excused from offences against natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of means is distinct from lack of diligence. Adults capable of governing their affairs are presumed to have means to know natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captivity or being under enemy power totally excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a man is captive or in the power of the enemy without his fault, the obligation of the law ceaseth; he must obey the enemy or die, so such obedience is no crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obedience under duress to avoid death or loss of livelihood is excused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsion by present terror of death totally excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: If by the terror of present death a man is compelled to do a fact against the law, he is totally excused; no law can oblige abandonment of self-preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even supposing an obligating law, natural reason supports preserving life when immediate choice is between doing the act or immediate death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity (destitution of food) totally excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man is destitute of food or other necessity and cannot preserve himself any other way than by committing an act against the law (e.g., taking food in famine), he is totally excused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survival necessity removes the nature of crime under Hobbes' account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor excused by authority of author (but not excused against third injured party)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts done against the law by the authority of another are by that authority excused against the author; but not excused against the third person injured; both author and actor are criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority absolves the actor insofar as the author cannot justly condemn his own command, but it does not remove liability toward those harmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign command contrary to former law excuses actor
rubrics_metrics.description: When the man or assembly with sovereign power commandeth a man to do that which is contrary to a former law, the doing of it is totally excused (as the command is an abrogation of the former law for that particular fact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects ought not to condemn acts commanded by sovereign; sovereign cannot justly be punished by others for such commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of crime measured on four scales
rubrics_metrics.description: The Degrees of Crime are measured First, by the malignity of the Source or Cause; Secondly, by the contagion of the Example; Thirdly, by the mischiefe of the Effect; and Fourthly, by the concurrence of Times, Places, and Persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This forms the general schema for aggravation and extenuation: motive, example effect, and circumstances determine degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of power aggravates crime
rubrics_metrics.description: The same Fact done against the Law, if it proceed from presumption of strength, riches, or friends to resist execution of the Law, is a greater Crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption of impunity by force breeds contempt of laws and is thus more dangerous than crimes committed from mere hope of escape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evil teachers' authority extenuates
rubrics_metrics.description: An error proceeding from the authority of a teacher, or interpreter of the law publicly authorised, is not so faulty as private error; public instruction resembling law may excuse more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an errored teaching comes from public authority it resembles law and can totally excuse in many cases not denying sovereign power or against evident law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of impunity extenuate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where precedent examples of impunity have existed, they provide hopes of impunity that partly excuse later offenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sovereign that creates such expectations (by failing to punish) shares in the blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premeditation aggravates
rubrics_metrics.description: A Crime arising from premeditation is greater than the same crime from sudden passion; premeditation shows contempt for law, punishment, and societal consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time between knowing the law and committing the act counts as deliberation; sudden passion is not total excuse but may mitigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit approbation by sovereign extenuates
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts which the law expressly condemn, but the law-maker tacitly approveth, are lesser crimes than those condemned both by law and lawmaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sovereign behavior implicitly approves acts contrary to written law (e.g., tolerating duels), some blame attaches to sovereign and reduces culpability of subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison by effects: harm to many is worse than harm to few
rubrics_metrics.description: The same fact is greater when it redounds to the damage of many than when it hurts few; crimes producing future contagious harm are greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: maintaining doctrines contrary to established religion is more blameworthy in an authorized preacher than in private person; reputation and imitation magnify crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes against the commonwealth (Laesae Majestas) are greater
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts of hostility against the present state of the Common-wealth are greater Crimes than the same acts done to private men; these are Crimina Laesae Majestatis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes betraying forts, revealing state secrets, attempts on representative authority, and acts to diminish authority present or future—design or act contrary to fundamental law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bribery and false testimony are greater crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Those Crimes which render Judgements of no effect (e.g., receiving money to give false judgement or testimony) are greater Crimes than otherwise deceiving a man of like or greater sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such crimes damage not only individuals but the legal system, enabling force and private revenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embezzlement (depeculation) of public treasure is greater
rubrics_metrics.description: Robbery and Depeculation of the Public treasure or Revenues is a greater Crime than robbing or defrauding a private man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To rob the public is to rob many at once; public finance crimes scale harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeiting public authority aggravates
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeiting usurpation of public ministery, public seals, or public coin is worse than counterfeiting a private man's person or seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fraud affecting public instruments harms many and corrupts public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of crimes against private persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Of facts against the Law done to private men, the greater Crime is that where the damage is most sensible in common opinion: e.g., to kill is a greater Crime than any other injury; to kill with torment is greater than simple killing; mutilation greater than spoiling goods; spoiling goods by terror/wounds greater than clandestine surreption; clandestine surreption greater than consent by fraud; violation of chastity by force greater than by flattery; married woman violated worse than unmarried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reflect common valuations; law regards the general inclination of mankind rather than particular sensitivities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravation by person, time, and place
rubrics_metrics.description: A Crime is much aggravated by the person, time, and place: e.g., killing one's parent is greater than killing another; robbing a poor man is worse than robbing a rich man; committing crime during time/place of devotion is greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors include relationships (parent), vulnerability (poor), sanctity of occasion (devotion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public crimes vs private crimes (pleas)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an accusation is in the name of the commonwealth, it is called a Publique Crime; when in the name of a private man, a Private Crime; pleas accordingly are public (Judicia Publica) or private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Who brings the accusation (sovereign vs private) determines the procedural character of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: "A PUNISHMENT, is an Evill inflicted by publique Authority, on him that hath done, or omitted that which is Judged by the same Authority to be a Transgression of the Law; to the end that the will of men may thereby the better be disposed to obedience."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment is a public-authority infliction with the aim of moving will toward obedience; this definition frames what counts as punishment vs other harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of the right to punish
rubrics_metrics.description: The Right which the Common-wealth hath to punish is not grounded on concession of subjects but on the pre-social right each person had to all things for preservation; in creating commonwealth they strengthen the sovereign to use his own right for preservation of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign power to punish derives from original natural right (state of nature) transferred in form to the sovereign for collective preservation, except limits set by natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private injuries and revenges are not punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither private revenges nor injuries of private men can properly be styled Punishment, because they proceed not from publique Authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private revenge lacks public-authority judgment and therefore is hostile act rather than punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of preferment is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: To be neglected and unpreferred by public favour is not a Punishment, because no new evil is thereby inflicted; he is left in the estate he was in before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of favour without active infliction of new harm is not punitive in Hobbes' sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evil inflicted without precedent public condemnation is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The evil inflicted by public authority without precedent public condemnation is not to be styled Punishment but an hostile act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment presupposes antecedent public judgment that the act was a transgression; extrajudicial harms are hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evil inflicted by usurped power is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil inflicted by usurped power, and judges without authority from the sovereign, is not Punishment but an act of hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only acts by legitimate sovereign authority count as punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evil inflicted without respect to future good is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: All evil inflicted without intention or possibility of disposing the delinquent or others to obey the laws is not Punishment but an act of hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment must have forward-looking corrective/disciplinary purpose; mere revenge lacks the qualifying end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural evil consequences are not human punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural harmful consequences (e.g., being slain in assault, suffering sickness from unlawful acts) are not punishments in respect of men because they are inflicted by nature, not by human authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divine/natural consequences differ from civil punishments; human law punishes by authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm less than the benefit of transgressing is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the harm inflicted be less than the benefit or contentment that naturally followeth the crime, that harm is not within the definition of Punishment and is rather the Price or Redemption than Punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment that fails to deter because benefit exceeds harm functions as a price, encouraging crime rather than deterring it.

rubrics_metrics.name: If law prescribes a penalty, later excess is hostility not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Punishment be determined and prescribed in the Law itself, and after the crime committed a greater Punishment is inflicted, the excess is not Punishment but an act of hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected addition to penalty undermines the deterrent effect and transforms excess into unlawful hostility. Where no prior punishment is determined, whatever is inflicted is punishment.
